s0101.literal: Upon leaving the sackcloth he was a Liang Grand Academy Doctor; he was gradually promoted to secretary in the outer military staff office of the Western Central Commander, Prince of Xiangdong, and together with Bao Quan of Donghai, Zong Lin of Nanyang, Liu Huan of Pingyuan, and Liu Yue of Pei commandery shared charge of secretarial records.
s0101.idiomatic: He entered office as a Liang grand-academy doctor, then rose to secretary on Prince Xiangdong's outer military staff, sharing record-keeping with Bao Quan of Donghai, Zong Lin of Nanyang, Liu Huan of Pingyuan, and Liu Yue of Pei.

s0102.literal: He entered [capital] service as Gentleman of the Ceremonies Bureau in the Masters of Writing.
s0102.idiomatic: He was made gentleman of the ceremonies bureau in the masters of writing.

s0103.literal: When the Prince of Xiangdong went out to govern the two provinces Jiang and Jing, [Hongzhi] was repeatedly promoted to recording secretary and advising aide, concurrently serving as magistrate of Chaisang and Dangyang counties.
s0103.idiomatic: When Prince Xiangdong took up Jiang and Jing, he was repeatedly made recording secretary and advising aide, and concurrently magistrate of Chaisang and Dangyang.

s0104.literal: When Emperor Yuan of Liang assumed the provisional regime, [he] was appointed acting-with-staff, stalwart-fruits general, and heir-apparent chief steward.
s0104.idiomatic: When Emperor Yuan of Liang assumed the provisional regime, he was made acting-with-staff bearer, stalwart-fruits general, and the heir's chief steward.

s0105.literal: Soon he was made wise-martial general and inner administrator of Hengyang.
s0105.idiomatic: He was soon made wise-martial general and inner administrator of Hengyang.

s0106.literal: He was transferred to steadfast-resolve general, chief steward of the Pacify-the-South [army], inner administrator of Changsha, acting in the prefectural and regional affairs of Xiangzhou, and enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiangbin county with a fief of six hundred households.
s0106.idiomatic: He became steadfast-resolve general, chief steward of the pacify-the-south army, inner administrator of Changsha, acting prefect of Xiangzhou, and marquis of Xiangbin with six hundred households.

s0107.literal: He successively served as administrator of Shaoling and Lingling, cloud-banner general, and inspector of Chang prefecture.
s0107.idiomatic: He served in turn as administrator of Shaoling and Lingling, cloud-banner general, and inspector of Chang.

s0108.literal: When Wang Lin raised troops, Hongzhi was in Xiangzhou; when Lin was defeated he returned to court.
s0108.idiomatic: When Wang Lin rebelled, Hongzhi was in Xiangzhou; after Lin's defeat he returned to court.

s0109.literal: In the Tianchen era he successively served as grand-academy doctor, chief steward to the Prince of Luling, left assistant in the Masters of Writing, concurrently superintendent of the Feathered Forest guard, palace scatterer grandee, and director of the Secretariat, in charge of the national history.
s0109.idiomatic: Under Tianchen he was in turn grand-academy doctor, chief steward to the prince of Luling, left assistant in the masters of writing, superintendent of the feathered forest guard, palace scatterer grandee, and director of the secretariat in charge of the national history.

s0110.literal: He was promoted to minister of rites and grand master for the glorious, with the added golden seal and purple ribbon.
s0110.idiomatic: He was promoted to minister of rites and grand master for the glorious, with golden seal and purple ribbon.

s0111.literal: In the seventh year of Taijian he fell ill and was near death; he left a memorial instructing his family: "From this year my sinews and strength have waned—I may truly be in decline—yet my love of life never quite knew itself; I only sought pleasure and did not notice old age approaching."
s0111.idiomatic: In Taijian year seven he fell gravely ill and left instructions for his household: "This year my strength has failed—I am plainly in decline—yet I never noticed how I clung to life; I only chased pleasure and did not see old age coming."

s0112.literal: Now the seasonal ordinance has come due; I shall be like morning dew. Seventy-odd years have largely been counted sufficient; raising my hand I take leave whole, with little regret.
s0112.idiomatic: "My time has come; I shall vanish like morning dew. Seventy-odd years are enough; I take my leave with scarcely a regret."

s0113.literal: After my breath is cut off, at once buy timber visible in the market; the timber must be of small form so it is easy to carry.
s0113.idiomatic: "After I die, buy whatever coffin wood is for sale in the market—it must be small enough to carry easily."

s0114.literal: Dress me in seasonal garments—an ancient common rule—but when I go below to meet my forebears I must observe full ritual: I may wear a single-layer skirt robe, jacket, shirt, and old shoes.
s0114.idiomatic: "Bury me in plain seasonal dress, as custom allows; but to meet my ancestors I need full propriety—only a single skirt-robe, jacket, shirt, and worn shoes."

s0115.literal: Since I should wait upon and nourish [them], there should be veil-cloths; or if I meet good friends, incense is needed again. In the coffin place only white cloth hand-towels and a coarse incense burner—beyond that nothing at all.
s0115.idiomatic: "Provide veil-cloths for their service, and incense if good friends come; put in the coffin only white cloth towels and a coarse censer—nothing else."

s0116.literal: He died at home, aged seventy-six.
s0116.idiomatic: He died at home, aged seventy-six.

s0117.literal: He had a collected works in twenty juan.
s0117.idiomatic: He left collected works in twenty juan.

s0119.literal: Yuan Xian, style Dezhi, was the younger brother of Yuan Shu, left vice director of the Masters of Writing.
s0119.idiomatic: Yuan Xian, styled Dezhi, was the younger brother of Yuan Shu, left vice director of the masters of writing.

s0120.literal: From youth he was clever and keen, loved learning, and had refined capacity.
s0120.idiomatic: As a boy he was bright and eager to learn, with a calm, generous bearing.

s0121.literal: Emperor Wu of Liang repaired and built the school precinct, separately opening five halls; one hall lay west of Xian's residence. Xian often summoned and led students, debating with them; whenever he had a new interpretation it exceeded people's expectations, and his peers all sighed in admiration.
s0121.idiomatic: When Emperor Wu of Liang rebuilt the schools and opened five halls, one stood west of Xian's house. He often gathered students to debate; his fresh readings surprised everyone, and his peers admired him.

s0122.literal: In the eighth year of Datong the Emperor composed section-and-clause commentary on the Correct Sayings of Confucius and ordered it sent down to the National University to proclaim the imperial meaning.
s0122.idiomatic: In Datong year eight the emperor finished his commentary on the Correct Sayings of Confucius and ordered the National University to expound the imperial interpretation.

s0123.literal: Xian was then fourteen and was summoned as a Correct Sayings student of the National University; he called on the libationer Dao Gai, who watched him departing and admired his spirit and bearing.
s0123.idiomatic: Xian was fourteen when he was made a Correct Sayings student at the National University. He visited libationer Dao Gai, who watched him leave and admired his bearing.

s0124.literal: After one year in study, National University doctor Zhou Hongzheng said to Xian's father Junzheng: "Does your worthy son wish to undergo the examination this year?"
s0124.idiomatic: After a year of study, National University doctor Zhou Hongzheng asked Xian's father Junzheng, "Will your worthy son sit for the examination this year?"

s0125.literal: Junzheng said: "His understanding of the classics is still shallow; I do not dare let him try."
s0125.idiomatic: Junzheng replied, "His classical learning is still shallow; I dare not let him try yet."

s0126.literal: After several days Junzheng sent his retainer Cen Wenhao with Xian to wait on Hongzheng. Meeting Hongzheng about to ascend the lecture seat with disciples all assembled, he brought Xian into the room, handed him a fly-whisk, and had Xian set forth the theme.
s0126.idiomatic: A few days later Junzheng sent his retainer Cen Wenhao with Xian to see Hongzheng. Hongzheng was about to lecture with all disciples present; he brought Xian in, gave him a fly-whisk, and told him to open the discussion.

s0127.literal: At that time Xie Qi and He Tuo were seated; Hongzheng said: "You two worthies, though you have exhausted the profound depths—will you not fear this young man!"
s0127.idiomatic: Xie Qi and He Tuo were in the audience. Hongzheng said, "You two have plumbed the depths—will you not fear this youth?"

s0128.literal: He and Xie then in turn raised points of doctrine, probing the utmost reaches of principle; Xian went back and forth several rounds, replying with ease and keenness.
s0128.idiomatic: He and Xie took turns pressing hard questions to the limits of doctrine; Xian answered several exchanges with easy, sharp replies.

s0129.literal: Hongzheng said to Tuo: "Ask as you please; do not measure him as a child."
s0129.idiomatic: Hongzheng told He Tuo, "Question him as you will—do not treat him as a child."

s0130.literal: At that time students filled the hall and onlookers piled in layers, yet Xian's expression was calm and his debate had surplus.
s0130.idiomatic: The hall was packed and spectators crowded in, yet Xian remained composed and still had answers to spare.

s0131.literal: Hongzheng repeatedly raised difficult points but in the end could not bend him; he therefore told Wenhao: "Go back and consult Administrator Yuan of Wu—this lad is already fit to replace me as doctor."
s0131.idiomatic: Hongzheng raised difficulty after difficulty but could not defeat him. He told Wenhao, "Tell Administrator Yuan of Wu that this boy is already fit to succeed me as doctor."

s0132.literal: At that time students answering policy questions often gave bribes; Wenhao asked to prepare the ritual gift; Junzheng said: "How could I use money to buy my son a place?"
s0132.idiomatic: Students then often bribed their way through policy examinations. Wenhao asked to prepare the ritual gift; Junzheng said, "Would I buy my son a degree with money?"

s0133.literal: The academic office bore a grudge.

s0134.literal: When Xian was examined, they all raised fierce difficulties; Xian answered each challenge as it came, analyzing like flowing water.
s0134.idiomatic: At Xian's examination they all pressed fierce questions; he answered on the spot, reasoning as fluently as flowing water.

s0135.literal: Dao Gai looked at Xian and said: "Yuan Junzheng truly has posterity."
s0135.idiomatic: Dao Gai looked at Xian and said, "Yuan Junzheng will have worthy descendants."

s0136.literal: When Junzheng was about to go to Wu commandery, Gai saw him off at the campaign-slayer pavilion and said to Junzheng: "Yesterday's policy candidates Xiao Minsun and Xu Xiaoke are not without understanding of doctrine, but in spirit, instrument, and bearing they fall far short of your worthy son."
s0136.idiomatic: When Junzheng was leaving for Wu commandery, Gai saw him off at the Campaign-Slayer Pavilion and said, "Yesterday's candidates Xiao Minsun and Xu Xiaoke know their texts, but in spirit and bearing they are far below your son."

s0137.literal: Soon he was ranked in the top grade.
s0137.idiomatic: He soon placed in the top grade.

s0138.literal: As a nobleman's son he was chosen to marry the Princess of Nan'a—the daughter of Liang's Emperor Jianwen.
s0138.idiomatic: As a nobleman's son he was chosen to marry Princess Nan'a, daughter of Liang's Emperor Jianwen.

s0139.literal: Xian was thoroughly versed in court regulations and especially clear in hearing and deciding cases; whenever the facts of a prison case were not exhausted but the clerks had already prepared the statutory penalty, he would seize leisure moments and often speak to the ruler about it—the cases he set right were very numerous.
s0139.idiomatic: Xian knew court law thoroughly and was especially skilled at judgment. When investigators had not finished a case but officials had already drafted the sentence, he would use spare moments to speak to the throne; the cases he corrected were very many.

s0140.literal: He once attended a feast in the Fragrant-Accepting Pavilion; after the guests withdrew, Emperor Gaozong kept Xian and the commandant of the guards Fan Jun, moved their seats to the mountain pavilion, and talked and feasted all day.
s0140.idiomatic: Once, after a banquet in the Fragrant-Accepting Pavilion, Emperor Gaozong kept Xian and commandant of the guards Fan Jun, moved to the mountain pavilion, and talked with them all day.

s0141.literal: Emperor Gaozong fixed his gaze on Xian and said to Jun, "The Yuan house has always produced men"; he was honored thus.
s0141.idiomatic: The emperor looked at Xian and told Fan Jun, "The Yuan family has always had real men in it"—such was the esteem in which he was held.

s0142.literal: In the fifth year he entered [capital service] as palace attendant.
s0142.idiomatic: In year five he became palace attendant.

s0143.literal: In the sixth year he was appointed administrator of Wu commandery; because his father held office he firmly declined and did not accept, and was instead made bright-martial general and inner administrator of Nankang.
s0143.idiomatic: In year six he was named administrator of Wu but declined because his father was in office; he was made bright-martial general and inner administrator of Nankang instead.

s0144.literal: In the ninth year his term ended; he was made scattered-cavalry regular attendant and concurrent minister of the board of civil office; soon after he held the full post.
s0144.idiomatic: When his term ended in year nine he became scattered-cavalry regular attendant and acting minister of personnel, then received the full appointment.

s0145.literal: Xian, having long occupied a pure and eminent post, repeatedly memorialized asking to be released from office.
s0145.idiomatic: Having long held a high, unsullied post, Xian repeatedly asked to resign.

s0146.literal: Emperor Gaozong said: "Others in office have often had defamatory memorials.
s0146.idiomatic: Emperor Gaozong said, "Others in office are often attacked in memorials.

s0147.literal: You have handled affairs for many years and may be called unsullied; I will separately note and reward you—do not decline."
s0147.idiomatic: You have served many years with a clean record; I will mark that separately—do not resign."

s0148.literal: In the thirteenth year he was promoted to right vice director, participating in selection affairs.
s0148.idiomatic: In year thirteen he was promoted to right vice director and took part in appointments.

s0149.literal: Earlier Xian's eldest brother Jianyi's son had been left vice director; now Xian was right vice director; within the secretariat they called Jianyi the great vice director and Xian the lesser vice director, and the court took pride in it.
s0149.idiomatic: His elder brother's son Jianyi had been left vice director; now Xian was right vice director. The secretariat called them the great and lesser vice directors, and the court took pride in the pair.

s0150.literal: When Emperor Gaozong fell ill, Xian and the minister of the board of civil office Mao Xi both received testamentary charge.
s0150.idiomatic: When Emperor Gaozong fell ill, Xian and minister of personnel Mao Xi both received his deathbed charge.

s0151.literal: When Prince Shixing Shulang committed his outrage, Xian directed deployments and took part with force.
s0151.idiomatic: When Prince Shixing Shulang rebelled, Xian directed the response and played a leading part in suppressing him.

s0152.literal: The Later Lord, wounded and gravely ill, grasped Xian's hand and said: "My son is still young; I entrust what follows to you."
s0152.idiomatic: The Later Lord, badly wounded, took Xian's hand and said, "My son is still young; I leave what follows to you."

s0153.literal: Xian said: "All hearts murmur in hope that Your Sagely Person will recover; as to testamentary charge, I dare not yet receive the edict."
s0153.idiomatic: Xian said, "All hearts pray for Your Majesty's recovery; I dare not yet accept a deathbed charge."

s0154.literal: For merit he was enfeoffed as Baron of Jian'an county with a fief of four hundred households, appointed concurrently chief aide to the crown prince; the rest remained as before.
s0154.idiomatic: For his service he was made baron of Jian'an with four hundred households and chief aide to the crown prince; his other posts were unchanged.

s0155.literal: Soon he was made palace attendant, trustworthy-martial general, and steward of the crown prince's household.
s0155.idiomatic: He was soon made palace attendant, trustworthy-martial general, and steward of the crown prince's household.

s0158.literal: [3] year, Sui armies came to attack; [8] Sui general He Ruobi advanced and burned the North Wing Gate of the palace city; palace guards all fled; court gentlemen gradually each withdrew—only Xian guarded and attended at the ruler's side.
s0158.idiomatic: In Zhenming year three the Sui invaded; [8] Sui general He Ruobi burned the palace city's north wing gate. Guards fled and courtiers drifted away—only Xian stayed at the emperor's side.

s0159.literal: The Later Lord said to Xian: "From the first I have treated you before others; seeing you today—one may say that in cold years one knows the pine and cypress are last to wither."
s0159.idiomatic: The Later Lord told Xian, "I have always favored you above others; today you prove that pines and cypresses are the last to fade in winter."

s0160.literal: The Later Lord in panic was about to hide; Xian with stern countenance said: "When the northern troops enter they certainly will not violate [you]; the great affair is thus—Your Majesty, be at peace."
s0160.idiomatic: As the emperor panicked and prepared to flee, Xian said sternly, "The northerners will not harm you. The matter is settled—Your Majesty, stay calm."

s0161.literal: Your servant wishes Your Majesty to straighten robes and cap, mount the front hall, and follow the precedent of Liang's Emperor Wu receiving Hou Jing.
s0161.idiomatic: "I beg Your Majesty to dress properly, sit in the front hall, and follow Emperor Wu of Liang's example when he received Hou Jing."

s0162.literal: The Later Lord did not follow; he thereupon left the couch and galloped away. Xian entered from the rear hall, Jingyang Palace; the Later Lord cast himself into a well; Xian bowed, wept, and withdrew.
s0162.idiomatic: The emperor refused, leapt from his couch, and fled. Xian went in through the rear Jingyang Palace hall; finding the emperor had thrown himself into a well, he bowed, wept, and withdrew.

s0163.literal: When the capital fell he entered Sui service; Sui appointed him bearer of the staff, commander of all military affairs in Chang prefecture, opener of the mansion equal in honor to the three dukes, and inspector of Chang prefecture.
s0163.idiomatic: After the capital fell he entered Sui service as bearer of the staff, commander of military affairs in Chang, opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes, and inspector of Chang.

s0164.literal: In the fourteenth year of Kaihuang an edict appointed him chief steward of the Prince of Jin's household.
s0164.idiomatic: In Kaihuang year fourteen he was made chief steward of the prince of Jin's household.

s0165.literal: In the eighteenth year he died, aged seventy.
s0165.idiomatic: He died in Kaihuang year eighteen, aged seventy.

s0166.literal: Posthumously he was made grand general and Duke of Ancheng commandery; posthumous title Jian.
s0166.idiomatic: Posthumously he was made grand general and duke of Ancheng, with the posthumous name Jian.

s0167.literal: His eldest son Chengjia served Sui to secretary aide and vice director of the National University.
s0167.idiomatic: His eldest son Chengjia served the Sui as secretary aide and vice director of the National University.

s0168.literal: The historian says: Emperor Yuan of Liang said that among scholar-officials he especially valued Zhou Hongzheng of Runan—how true those words are!
s0168.idiomatic: The historian writes: Emperor Yuan of Liang said that among scholar-officials he especially valued Zhou Hongzheng of Runan—how true that was!

s0169.literal: Observing his refined capacity and elevated standards, especially his mastery of arcane discourse, he was also a national teacher of a generation.
s0169.idiomatic: In breadth of mind and mastery of arcane learning he was a national teacher of his age.

s0170.literal: Yuan Xian's style was ordered and severe; he followed righteousness and trod the Way.
s0170.idiomatic: Yuan Xian's manner was austere and upright; he lived by duty and the Way.

s0171.literal: Han Fei said that when a man as minister commits his person [to a lord], his heart has no second [loyalty].
s0171.idiomatic: Han Fei said that when a minister pledges himself to his lord, his heart must not be divided.

s0172.literal: Xian did not swerve from start to finish—truly praiseworthy.
s0172.idiomatic: Xian never wavered from first to last—worthy of praise indeed.

s0174.literal: [1] A man of Ancheng in Runan

s0176.literal: Deleted according to the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions.
s0176.idiomatic: Deleted per the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions.

s0179.literal: [uncle] the Attendant-in-Ordinary and Protector-General She raised them—changed according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0179.idiomatic: On "[uncle] Attendant-in-Ordinary and Protector-General She raised them"—emended per the History of the Southern Dynasties.

s0180.literal: Comment: the biography of Zhou She in the History of the Southern Dynasties has the phrase "his nephew Hongzheng"—thus Zhou She was Hongzheng's paternal uncle.
s0180.idiomatic: The Southern Dynasties biography of Zhou She calls Hongzheng his nephew; She was therefore Hongzheng's uncle.

s0181.literal: [3] Sent out as magistrate of Ye—Qian Daxin's Examination of Discrepancies in the Twenty-Two Histories says: "The location of Liang's Ye county is uncertain."
s0181.idiomatic: On "sent out as magistrate of Ye": Qian Daxin's Examination of the Twenty-Two Histories says the site of Liang's Ye county is unknown.

s0182.literal: He also cites Yuan Tingchu: "'Ye' is probably the character for 'Yin.'"
s0182.idiomatic: He cites Yuan Tingchu: "Ye is probably Yin."

s0185.literal: [3] year the Heir Apparent Zhao Ming died—comment: the Heir Apparent Zhao Ming died in the third year of Zhong Datong; the character "zhong" is now supplied and "two" is changed to "three."
s0185.idiomatic: On "[3] year the Heir Apparent Zhao Ming died": Zhao Ming died in Zhong Datong year three; zhong is supplied and two is changed to three.

s0186.literal: The History of the Southern Dynasties also lacks "zhong"; the character "three" is not in error.
s0186.idiomatic: The Southern Dynasties history also omits zhong; three is correct.

s0189.literal: [sui] antiquity—changed according to the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions.
s0189.idiomatic: On "[sui] antiquity"—emended per the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions.

s0190.literal: [6] Chief steward of the Prince of Nanping's mansion in Xin prefecture—when the Prince of Nanping was inspector of Yangzhou, Que as chief steward acted in Yangzhou affairs; whence a "Xin prefecture"?
s0190.idiomatic: On "chief steward of Prince Nanping's mansion in Xin prefecture": Nanping was then inspector of Yangzhou and Que acted for Yangzhou—why Xin prefecture?

s0191.literal: According to the biography of Prince Nanping Yi, in the first year of Zhide Yi was made trustworthy-martial general; "Xin prefecture" is probably an error for "trustworthy-martial."
s0191.idiomatic: Prince Nanping Yi's biography shows him made trustworthy-martial general in Zhide year one; Xin prefecture is probably a corruption of trustworthy-martial.

s0192.literal: [7] From the first year of Zhide to performing the libation ceremony—comment: according to the annals of the Later Lord, the crown prince received the capping rite in the seventh month of Zhide year two, and performed the libation ceremony in the twelfth month of year three.
s0192.idiomatic: On "from Zhide year one to performing the libation ceremony": the Later Lord's annals place the crown prince's capping in Zhide year two, month seven, and the libation in year three, month twelve.

s0195.literal: [3] year Sui armies came to attack—comment: according to He Ruobi's crossing the river to Jiankang, this was the third year of Zhenming; "yuan" is an error for the character "three"; now corrected.
s0195.idiomatic: On "[3] year Sui armies came to attack": He Ruobi crossed to Jiankang in Zhenming year three; yuan is a corruption of three; emended.
